newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-CFTC chief sees progress in reform talks.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-CFTC chief sees progress in reform talks.

text.p: U.S. futures regulators have made "some progress" in negotiations to find a compromise to proposed legislation that would strip the Commodity Futures Trading Commission of much of its regulatory power, the head of the CFTC said on Thursday.
CFTC chairwoman Brooksley Born said in an interview with Reuters that the talks were continuing and that lawmakers had imposed no deadline for the parties to reach a compromise.

Born said the CFTC has been talking with various interested parties, ranging from other government agencies to the exchanges to commodity professionals to the users of markets, including agricultural organizations.
"We have made some progress in these discussions," she said. "They (the talks) are ongoing," she added.

Richard Lugar, an Indiana Republican, and Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat, who co-sponsored the bill in the Senate, last spring urged the CFTC and the futures exchanges to work out a compromise to the proposed legislation, which would deregulate 90 percent of the U.S. futures market.

The so-called "pro market" exemption would remove all traders with a net worth of more than $1 million from CFTC supervision, and eliminate most of the exchanges' recordkeeping, market surveillance and auditing requirements.
The Senate Agriculture committee had planned to mark-up the legislation last month, but postponed it in the hope that the industry and regulators could reach an agreement.

Born has repeatedly said that the proposed legislation goes too far and could lead to market manipulation. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and several farm groups also oppose the creation of a professional market.

As a peace offering, Born said the CFTC was willing to ease some regulatory burdens or modify the fast-track program rolled out by the agency last January that was designed to speed up agency approval of new contracts.
"We would be willing to potentially revisit some elements if they are thought to be onerous regulatory aspects of that program that are not justified by the public interest," Born said.
Before the CFTC adopted the fast-track procedure, the agency spent an average of 90 days studying a new contract proposal.

So far, only the Chicago Board of Trade has used the 10- or 45-day fast-track process. The CBOT requested approval of four new contracts to trade futures and options tied to the U.S. inflation index and five-year Treasury bonds, Born said.
"We also are in the process of trying to streamline our regulations and modernize them and would be open to a compromise that called for a general streamlining of the existing markets," she said.

The exchanges have pushed hard for the legislation, insisting that the CFTC must be reined in for them to compete with fast-growing futures exchanges in other countries. They worry that overseas exchanges will siphon away business.

"The basic issue that we can't seem to agree on is whether the exchanges can be trusted to continue keeping records and data about trades," said a representative with one of the Chicago exchanges, speaking on condition of anonymity. "What the CFTC doesn't seem to remember is that it's in our own best interest to preserve investor confidence in the market."
At the same time that U.S. lawmakers are mulling over dismantling the CFTC, other countries are trying to duplicate the U.S.-style regulations imposed by the CFTC.

"In other countries they are moving away from self-regulatory activity on the part of exchanges," Born said. "The U.S. regulatory regime for futures is the model that is widely accepted internationally... To a large extent the pending legislation would be a repudiation of that."

Attempts to reach a compromise on the legislation have also been complicated by several other issues involved in the bills. The CFTC and the Treasury Department disagree over the bill's plan to clarify the so-called Treasury Amendment, which exempts foreign currency and government securities transactions from regulation.
